title: Given the root of a binary tree, return the values of the nodes you can see when looking at the tree from the right side, ordered from top to bottom.
shortTitle: Binary Tree Right Side View — BFS taking last node per level

s1_definition.profdef: The right side view of a binary tree is the set of nodes visible when viewing the tree from the right, which is exactly the rightmost node on each level. A breadth-first traversal processes the tree level by level, and for each level you capture the last node processed, which is the one visible from the right.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine standing to the right of the bank's org chart and seeing only the person furthest to the right on each rank. The top manager is visible, then on the next rank only the rightmost report is visible because the others are hidden behind them, and so on down the chart. The right side view is that list of rightmost people, one per rank.
s1_definition.oneliner: Do a level-order traversal and record the last node of each level, which is the rightmost one visible from the right.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The right side view of a binary tree is the set of nodes visible when viewing the tree from the right, which is exactly the rightmost node on each level. A breadth-first traversal processes the tree level by level, and for each level you capture the last node processed, which is the one visible from the right.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine standing to the right of the bank's org chart and seeing only the person furthest to the right on each rank. The top manager is visible, then on the next rank only the rightmost report is visible because the others are hidden behind them, and so on down the chart. The right side view is that list of rightmost people, one per rank.

**One line to remember:** Do a level-order traversal and record the last node of each level, which is the rightmost one visible from the right.

sections.s2_technical:
This is a direct application of level order traversal with a small twist: instead of collecting every node on a level, you keep only the one that is rightmost. Using the level-size snapshot technique, the rightmost node is simply the last one you process in that level's loop.

You begin by enqueuing the root if it exists. For example: `if (root != null) queue.offer(root);`.

You loop while the queue is not empty, snapshotting the level size at the start of each iteration. For example: `int levelSize = queue.size();`.

Inside the level loop you dequeue each node and enqueue its children, and you detect the last node of the level by checking the loop index. For example: `for (int i = 0; i < levelSize; i++) { Node n = queue.poll(); if (i == levelSize - 1) result.add(n.val); if (n.left != null) queue.offer(n.left); if (n.right != null) queue.offer(n.right); }`.

The condition that the index equals level size minus one picks exactly the rightmost node, because nodes are processed left to right within a level. Enqueuing left before right preserves that order.

The time complexity is linear because each node is enqueued and dequeued once, and the space is proportional to the maximum width of the tree. A senior nuance is the depth-first alternative: a traversal that visits the right child before the left, carrying the current depth, records the first node seen at each new depth, which is also the rightmost. Both are linear; the breadth-first version is more intuitive and maps naturally onto the level concept, while the depth-first version uses less memory on wide, shallow trees. A subtlety is that a left node can be visible if there is no right node at its level, which both approaches handle correctly because they track rightmost-per-level, not merely right children.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, the escalation hierarchy is a tree, and for an emergency contact sheet the operations team wants the most senior fallback contact at each escalation level, modeled as the rightmost node per level. This is exactly how Right Side View works.

Problem 2 — At some levels the rightmost branch may be missing, and the visible contact is then a left node, which must still be captured. This is exactly why the algorithm tracks the last node processed per level rather than only right children.

The mini-project builds an `EscalationNode` class, a `RightViewService` with a BFS that records the last node per level and logging, and a runnable demo over an escalation tree.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is the escalation tree rooted at CEO.

Step 1: CEO is enqueued. The level size is one. CEO is the only node and also the last, so CEO is added to the view. Its children RegionA and RegionB are enqueued.

Step 2: The level size is two. The loop processes RegionA first at index zero, not the last, so it is not added, but its right child DeskA2 is enqueued. Then it processes RegionB at index one, which is the last, so RegionB is added to the view, and its right child DeskB2 is enqueued. The queue now holds DeskA2 and DeskB2.

Step 3: The level size is two. It processes DeskA2 at index zero, not last, and enqueues its left child ClerkA3. Then it processes DeskB2 at index one, the last, so DeskB2 is added to the view. DeskB2 has no children. The queue now holds only ClerkA3.

Step 4: The level size is one. ClerkA3 is the only node and the last, so ClerkA3 is added to the view, even though it is a left child, because it is the rightmost node on its level. It has no children, so the queue empties.

Step 5: The right side view is CEO, RegionB, DeskB2, ClerkA3, correctly including the left node ClerkA3 that is visible because nothing is to its right on that level.

```text
2026-10-26T19:50:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Escalation Right-Side View
2026-10-26T19:50:00Z [INFO] Emergency fallback contacts (right-side view) = [CEO, RegionB, DeskB2, ClerkA3]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
             CEO            ← level0 last = CEO 
            /    \
        RegionA  RegionB    ← level1 last = RegionB 
          \         \
        DeskA2     DeskB2   ← level2 last = DeskB2 
          /
      ClerkA3               ← level3 last = ClerkA3  (a LEFT node!)

  BFS queue, record i == levelSize-1 each level:
    [CEO] → CEO
    [RegionA, RegionB] → RegionB
    [DeskA2, DeskB2] → DeskB2
    [ClerkA3] → ClerkA3
  view = [CEO, RegionB, DeskB2, ClerkA3]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The right side view of a binary tree is simply the rightmost node on each level, which is what you would see standing to the right of the tree. This maps directly onto a level-order traversal, so I use a breadth-first search with the level-size snapshot technique, and the rightmost node is just the last one I process within each level's loop. I enqueue the root, loop while the queue is not empty, snapshot the level size at the start of each iteration, and inside the loop I add a node to the result precisely when its index equals the level size minus one.

Because I enqueue left children before right children, nodes are processed left to right within a level, so the last-index condition reliably picks the rightmost node. The complexity is linear since each node is enqueued and dequeued once, and the space is proportional to the maximum width of the tree.

The subtlety I always call out is that a left node can be part of the view. If a level has no right-side branch, the rightmost node on that level is whatever left node is furthest right, and tracking the last node processed per level handles that automatically, whereas naively following only right children would miss it. I also mention the depth-first alternative that visits the right child first and records the first node seen at each new depth, which is equally correct and uses less memory on wide, shallow trees.

In my project at National Bank of India, I used this to build an emergency contact sheet from the escalation hierarchy, where the team wanted the most senior fallback contact at each escalation level, modeled as the rightmost node per level. Some levels had a missing right branch, so the visible contact there was a left node, and because the algorithm captures the last node processed per level rather than only right children, the contact sheet correctly included those left-side fallbacks.
